questions.question: A user mentions their diet at turn 5 of a 40-turn chat. A token window keeps the last 300 tokens. What happens to the diet?
options: It stays because it is important
It is dropped with the other old messages, unless something else keeps it
It moves to the end of the history
questions.explanation: A window keeps only the newest messages. Summaries and long-term memory exist to keep facts like this.

questions.question: What does one 'fold' of the summary buffer do?
options: Passes the previous summary plus the oldest messages to the summarizer and replaces the summary with its output
Moves the summary to a database
questions.explanation: Each fold is one summarizer call, usually a model call you pay for.

questions.question: The 600-character notes summary kept every planted fact. Why is it still a problem?
options: It kept the old budget next to the new one, so the model has to guess which is current
questions.explanation: Append-only summaries keep stale facts. A recall score alone would have called this a success.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of a structured summary with named slots?
options: Each slot has one current value, so updates replace old values and missing facts are visible
questions.explanation: The cost is choosing slots in advance; facts that fit no slot are lost.

questions.question: How should you test a summarization memory?
options: Read a few summaries and check they look fluent
Plant facts (including an update) in a long test conversation and check which current facts are in the final context
Ask the model if it remembers
questions.explanation: Summaries fail silently and still read well. Planted facts make the failure measurable.

questions.question: After several folds, the summary says 'staying at a hotel in the old town' instead of 'the Alfama hotel'. What is this called?
options: Drift: each rewrite paraphrases the previous summary and details blur
questions.explanation: Repeated rewriting loses precision. Keeping exact values in slots reduces drift.
